name: Wishful thinking
statement: People forecast the outcome they want, and the pull is strong when they are asked which outcome will happen and weak when they are asked how likely it is.
meaning: The claim is that a preference moves a forecast, not that some people are cheerful. A card is drawn from a deck of stated composition, or a football match is played, and the forecaster controls neither. Desirability bias is the gap between what such a forecaster says when the outcome pays them and what an otherwise identical forecaster says when it costs them. Optimism bias is a different claim, about a person's own prospects, and it usually needs a comparison with peers before it can be measured at all. Motivated reasoning is a third, and it says the evidence is read differently depending on what the reader wants. Wishful thinking as tested here survives the evidence being read correctly, because a person can state the outcome they prefer while knowing the odds against it.

origin.note: Krizan and Windschitl describe the study: children saw five pairs of card packs holding .1, .3, .5, .7 or .9 picture cards, one pack of each pair winning them a point and the other losing one, and were asked before each draw whether they expected to pick a picture. Windschitl and colleagues credit the marked-card paradigm to this paper. Marks was left out of the review's own synthesis as a clear outlier and as its only sample of children.

evidence: Windschitl, Smith, Rose and Krizan rebuilt the marked-card task with the experimenter blind to what each card was worth. Fifteen undergraduates saw decks of ten and predicted which of two markings would be drawn. They picked the critical mark 68.7% of the time when it paid $1, 50.0% when it paid nothing and 38.0% when it cost $1, F(2, 13) = 9.69, p < .01. The gap was widest on decks split five and five. Experiment 4 divided 46 undergraduates by response format. Those making a dichotomous prediction picked the critical mark 72.3%, 48.2% and 37.7% of the time across the three values, F(2, 20) = 12.85, p < .001. Those marking a continuous likelihood scale gave 52.8%, 50.2% and 47.8%, which the paper calls borderline, F(2, 22) = 2.82, p = .08. Experiment 5 put both formats to the same 44 people: a scale asking for their assessment showed nothing, F(2, 42) = 1.18, p > .20, while a scale asking for their hunch showed the bias, F(2, 42) = 15.82, p < .001. They add that the hunch effect ran between the $1 gain condition and the other two, and that likelihood judgements did not differ between the $0 and the loss conditions, p > .20. Field evidence comes from Simmons and Massey, who offered 770 NFL fans a $5 or $50 gift certificate for correctly picking the winner of one game. Partisans predicted their own team 78.4% of the time, chi-square(1) = 131.11, p < .001, and the rate held between the $5 and $50 groups, 81.0% against 75.7%, chi-square(1) = 1.64, p = .20. Massey, Simmons and Armor had earlier collected predictions from NFL fans in every week of the 2008 season, and report in their abstract that bias about preferred teams lasted the whole season, as strong after four months as after four weeks.

replication.headline: Ask people to name a winner and the effect appears almost every time. Ask the same people for a probability and it mostly vanishes.
replication.detail: Krizan and Windschitl sorted the experimental literature into four cells, by whether the event was a matter of chance and by whether the forecast was a discrete outcome or a likelihood judgement. Their Fig. 1 in the later paper counts the studies located: 14 asked for a discrete prediction about a chance event and 13 found the bias, 9 asked for a likelihood judgement about a chance event and 2 found it, 7 asked for a likelihood judgement about a non-chance event and 4 found it, and none had asked for a discrete prediction about a non-chance event. The review's own syntheses pool fewer samples than those counts, because effect sizes could not be computed for every study. Across 12 samples and 841 people, chance-event predictions gave OR = 2.26, 95% CI 1.89 to 2.71. Across 9 samples and 286 people, chance-event likelihood judgements gave g = 0.01, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.12. Across 5 of the 7 naturalistic studies, the two left out being null ones, 409 people gave g = 0.20, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.31. Windschitl and colleagues then filled the empty cell, and found nothing there: 39 people predicting answers to hard trivia questions gave 57.9%, 54.0% and 52.3% across the three values, F(2, 37) = 1.17, p > .20, against a clear effect in the card condition of the same study, F(2, 13) = 7.66, p < .01. Park, Windschitl, Miller, Smith, Stuart and Biangmano tested the format difference on staged contests. Among 269 students watching a basketball game, 75.4% of those asked to predict backed the team they had been assigned, and the format by team interaction gave OR = 8.51, Wald chi-square(1) = 14.93, p < .001. A second study recruited 331 students to watch an endurance race and analysed 314 after 17 failed a preregistered memory check. The rate was 82.4% for predictions, 67.6% for a dichotomous likelihood judgement and 64.7% for a continuous one, chi-square(1) = 6.13, p = .013 and chi-square(1) = 8.50, p = .004. Note that the likelihood judgements in that race were themselves biased, which the card studies had not found. The same laboratory has since taken the effect outside pure chance. Windschitl, Miller, Park, Rule, Clary and Smith ran six preregistered studies on car races and grid games where the uncertainty was part chance and part ignorance, and combined them at d = 1.11, Z = 5.88, p < .001, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.48. The bias was larger where the evidence for the two outcomes was of similar strength, d = 0.35, Z = 3.36, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.55, and stochasticity did not moderate it overall, d = 0.12, Z = 1.54, p = .123. Smith, Windschitl and Crawley recruited 345 Americans on MTurk a day before the 2020 presidential election and analysed the 329 with a preferred candidate. Trump supporters picked Trump 81.8% of the time and Biden supporters picked Biden 86.1% of the time, F(1, 323) = 264.34, p < .001, partial eta-squared 0.450, 90% CI 0.386 to 0.505, and the split was almost as wide on probability estimates, F(1, 323) = 178.26, p < .001, partial eta-squared 0.365. That study set out to repeat a debiasing result and failed: neither perspective-taking condition shifted the link, and an equivalence test bounded at a third of the effect Rose and Aspiras reported found the observed interaction smaller than that bound. The one entry the FORRT replication database holds in this area is also a failure. De Molière and Harris ran five experiments against Vosgerau's account of wishful thinking as misattributed arousal, and their abstract reports a Bayesian meta-analysis supporting the null.

study.cite: Windschitl, P. D., Smith, A. R., Rose, J. P., & Krizan, Z. (2010). The desirability bias in predictions: Going optimistic without leaving realism. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 111(1), 33-47.

limits: No multi-site or registered replication of the marked-card paradigm was found. A search on 17 August 2026 covered the FORRT replication database, Crossref, PubMed and the publication lists of the two laboratories that run this work, at Iowa and Appalachian State. The laboratory samples are small: 15 in the first experiment that rebuilt the paradigm, 15 in the card condition and 39 in the trivia condition of the second, then 30, 46 and 44. The trivia sample was topped up after an interim analysis of the first 30 participants showed a null. No structured effect size is recorded here because the five experiments report F tests and condition percentages rather than effect sizes, and the meta-analytic figures above belong to a review of other people's studies rather than to a replication of the entry's own study. Windschitl and colleagues read their own results as biased guessing rather than biased belief, which caps what the marked-card evidence can be asked to carry. Where a likelihood judgement is the measure, they point to a competing pull towards bracing for bad news. Preference was assigned by the experimenter only in the laboratory work. In the two NFL studies and the election study it was measured, so those results carry the confounds that follow, and Krizan and Windschitl warn that a desirability manipulation can move prior expectations along with desire.
misreadings: The name suggests someone believing what they want to be true. The strongest evidence shows something narrower: people asked to name an outcome name the one they want, while their stated probabilities stay close to the odds. Windschitl and colleagues call that going optimistic without leaving realism. It is not optimism bias, which concerns a person's own prospects and needs a peer comparison to be measured. It is not motivated reasoning either, which claims the evidence is read differently, since the card players in these studies were told exactly how many cards carried each mark. Nor is it only cheap talk. Simmons and Massey found the effect among the 313 fans, 41% of their sample, whose answers to four follow-up questions showed they believed their own prediction, OR = 3.27, p < .001. They also concede that a small share of their respondents backed their team without fully believing the prediction. The elusiveness has a pedigree of its own: Bar-Hillel and Budescu titled their series of tests The Elusive Wishful Thinking Effect, and the follow-up chapter with Amar on World Cup forecasts was called Still Elusive.
